name: Orthotropics

lead: Orthotropics is an approach to facial growth developed by British orthodontist John Mew, who held that resting tongue posture, mouth breathing and soft-food diets shape the jaws and face. Its popular offshoot is mewing, in which the tongue rests against the roof of the mouth, aimed at a more defined jaw and midface.

It is a major reference point in looksmaxxing communities. Proponents say the tongue, lips and jaws acting together influence how facial bones develop, and that malocclusion is largely environmental. Mainstream orthodontic bodies say evidence is inadequate, and a small study of 12 pairs of identical twins is among the few published comparisons.

paras: People practise tongue and lip posture and breathing habits daily, often starting in childhood or teens. Treatment in the approach can include palate expansion followed by a postural appliance (Mew's Biobloc system).

Posture exercises are widely discussed as low-risk, though forum users report jaw or joint discomfort. Mike Mew faced a misconduct process in the UK involving harm claims by child patients' families, and orthodontic appliances carry their usual risks.

web.title: Mewing: Social Media's Alternative to Orthognathic Surgery? (PubMed)

angle.text: Followers of John Mew's orthotropics, the root of mewing, hold that tongue posture and oral habits shape the jaw and midface during growth, and adopt it for a more defined face. Mainstream orthodontic bodies say evidence for the facial effect is inadequate.

lead: Orthotropics is a theory and treatment approach founded by British orthodontist John Mew (1928 to 2025). It holds that the resting posture and function of the tongue, lips and jaws influence facial growth, and that crooked teeth and a recessed face are largely environmental rather than inherited [1][2]. For people interested in their appearance, its promise is a more forward midface, a broader palate, a better-defined jaw and a straighter smile reached through posture and growth guidance rather than extractions, headgear or surgery. Mew framed the idea as the 'tropic premise' in 1958 [1][2].

The approach reached a mass audience as 'mewing', a do-it-yourself form of oral posture training named after John Mew and his son, orthodontist Mike Mew. Mew described it in plain terms as 'stand up straight and shut your mouth' [2]. Google Trends interest rose from January 2019, and videos on YouTube and TikTok have since carried the idea to a large audience, particularly in looksmaxxing communities [3][4]. Clinical orthotropic treatment, as practised in Mew's Biobloc system, combines palate expansion with a postural appliance and posture training [1].

Mainstream orthodontic organisations and reviewers say evidence for orthotropics is inadequate and that it is not a viable alternative to orthognathic surgery [1][3][5][6]. A small comparison of 12 pairs of identical twins, authored by Mew himself, is among the few published studies of the method [7]. The practice's founders have been the subject of regulatory proceedings in the UK, which is a recurring theme in media coverage [2][8][9].

paras: John Roland Chandley Mew was born on 7 September 1928 in Royal Tunbridge Wells, Kent. He studied dentistry at University College London from 1948, qualified in 1953 and completed a specialty in orthognathic surgery at the Queen Victoria Hospital in East Grinstead in 1956 [2]. He held office in the Southern Counties Branch of the British Dental Association and a visiting professorship in Timisoara, Romania [2].

Wikipedia reports that Mew became concerned about the facial outcomes of some conventional orthodontic cases and concluded that extractions, fixed appliances with elastics and retractive headgear could harm facial growth. In 1958 he put forward the Tropic Premise, which treated malocclusion as a postural deformity rather than mainly an inherited condition [2]. After a 1968 visit to Rolf Fraenkel in East Germany, who introduced him to the work of Konstantin Buteyko on breathing, he developed what he called facial growth guidance, or orthotropics, and the Biobloc treatment system [2]. He co-founded the International Association of Facial Growth Guidance in Fort Worth, Texas, in 1987 [2].

Mew's other interests, according to the same biography, included motor racing in the 1950s and 1960s, sailing, and building Braylsham Castle in Sussex between 1993 and 1999. He died at the castle on 25 June 2025, aged 96 [2].

John Mew's son, Michael Gordon Mew, is an orthodontist who has run a private clinic offering orthotropic treatment and has been the public face of mewing on social media and in interviews [3][9]. Wikipedia reports that he appeared in mainstream media in 2019 and was expelled from the British Orthodontic Society around that time for continuing to advocate his father's positions [2].

The central claim is that malocclusion is mainly caused by environment and posture. Wikipedia reports that Mew argued a tongue resting on the palate provides an outward force that widens the upper jaw in a growing child and prevents the maxilla from growing downward and backward, gradually producing a natural correction of crowding [2]. Mainstream orthodontics, by contrast, attributes crooked teeth primarily to genetics [2].

Orthotropic writing links this to modern lifestyle. Proponents argue that soft processed diets, bottle feeding, mouth breathing and low tongue posture leave modern jaws narrower and less forward than in earlier populations, producing crowded teeth, a recessed midface and a weak chin [10]. A 1992 article by Mew proposed that tongue and oral posture might also influence oropharyngeal development and middle ear aeration [11].

A science-magazine summary notes that supporters also attribute reduced jaw pain, easier breathing and relief from snoring to correct tongue posture, and that the idea resonates with the observation that human jaws have become smaller over time; Science Focus quotes dentist Kam Aulak saying rigorous studies of mewing itself are lacking [12]. Discover magazine reported that a 2020 BioScience paper on shrinking modern jawlines recommended harder foods and breathing and swallowing exercises, which it described as partly in line with the Mews' ideas without validating mewing's claimed benefits [4].

Clinical orthotropics, as described on Wikipedia, uses a palate-expanding appliance followed by a postural appliance (the Biobloc system), together with diet change and training of the resting tongue position [2]. Treatment is aimed at children whose faces are still growing; proponents say earlier intervention gives larger effects.

Mewing is the self-directed form. In general terms it means resting the tongue against the roof of the mouth, keeping the lips closed and breathing through the nose, with some practitioners also describing neck and head posture cues [4]. Discover reported that some advocates describe short practice sessions while others suggest keeping the posture all day [4]. Looksmax.org guides add related techniques such as 'intraoral face pulling' and appliances to the basic posture [10].

The Orthotropics YouTube channel and Mew's websites are named by forum members as the entry point to the subject; one looksmax.org member writes that their looksmaxxing journey began on the orthotropics website [13]. Interest in mewing began rising in January 2019 according to Google Trends, and Wikipedia reports that the practice has since had wide media coverage because of viral spread on YouTube and TikTok [3]. Wikipedia cites a 2019 Guardian explainer on the YouTube craze and a New York Times Magazine piece on two British orthodontists popular with incel communities [3].

Wikipedia describes mewing as especially popular in incel and looksmaxxing subcultures and links it to the 'brain rot' meme culture; it also notes 2024 coverage of students mewing in class to avoid answering questions [3]. Discover reported that TikTok videos on the subject have gathered hundreds of millions of views [4].

Within looksmax.org, orthotropics is treated as a discipline of its own, written 'orthotropics/dontics' (orthotropics plus orthodontics). Members post long personal plans and reading lists and recommend textbooks alongside the Orthotropics channel's videos [14][13]. One teenage member's plan thanks other forum users for helping to organise it [14].

A study published in 2007 in the World Journal of Orthodontics compared facial changes in 12 pairs of identical twins treated 10 years earlier, with one twin receiving fixed appliances and the other orthotropic growth-guidance treatment without fixed appliances. A panel of 12 lay judges rated the facial changes. The abstract reports that most orthotropically treated twins were judged to have improved while most conventionally treated twins were judged less attractive, that dental results differed little, and that conventionally treated cases appeared to relapse more often [7]. PubMed lists John Mew as the author, and the abstract notes that few comparative studies of this type exist [7]. Wikipedia describes the evidence for orthotropic efficacy as inadequate [1].

The 1992 article in the Journal of Laryngology and Otology proposed that tongue and oral posture might influence oropharyngeal development and middle ear aeration. It is a perspective piece rather than a trial [11]. A 2014 letter in the British Dental Journal titled 'Orthotropics: will we never be free?' addressed the controversy within the profession [15].

A 2019 article in the Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery by Lee, Graves and Friedlander, 'Mewing: Social Media's Alternative to Orthognathic Surgery?', examined the trend; Discover reports that it found no research supporting mewing as an alternative to orthodontics or jaw surgery [5][4]. No randomised controlled trial of mewing in adults has been published.

Wikipedia reports that most orthodontists do not consider mewing a viable alternative to jaw surgery and that the American Association of Orthodontists (AAO) has said there is no evidence it improves the jaw [3]. In a January 2024 press release, AAO president Myron Guymon said that tongue posture plays a role in oral health and development but that mewing 'oversimplifies the complexities of facial structure' [6].

The AAO release lists possible risks as loosened teeth, bite misalignment, tooth wear and speech changes from chronic pressure, and advises against relying on online trends to alter facial features [6]. Science Focus quotes Kam Aulak as saying too much force could strain the jaw, neck or facial muscles [12].

Wikipedia notes that Mew's theory contains some plausible conclusions but that evidence for its efficacy is inadequate [2]. Research on tongue posture in healthy adults is limited; more of it concerns orofacial myofunctional therapy in patients with breathing or sleep problems [12].

Wikipedia reports that the NHS fined John Mew for inappropriate treatment and that in 1987 he won a High Court appeal in which Lord Justice Murray Stuart-Smith found the criticisms unwarranted [2]. In 2010 the General Dental Council reprimanded him over advertisements it said denigrated orthodontics and misstated the GDC's position; Mew did not dispute the charge and called himself a whistleblower [2]. Wikipedia states that his licence was revoked in 2017 over false advertising and breach of patient confidentiality [2].

Mike Mew's case was heard by the GDC Professional Conduct Committee, which on 6 November 2024 found his fitness to practise impaired by misconduct and erased his name from the Dentists' Register [9]. Trade press reported that the panel found he had used approaches not sufficiently supported by scientific evidence that were liable to cause harm, and had made misleading statements about the need for treatment [8]. The case concerned two young patients, and a boy treated in 2018 was reported by the BBC to have had prolonged seizure-like episodes after extended use of devices [8].

A High Court appeal judgment dated 15 May 2026 records charges covering treatment and claims between September 2013 and May 2019, including a September 2017 YouTube video whose claims, among them that the treatment could increase a child's intelligence, the committee found misleading [9]. The judge rejected the grounds challenging the committee's handling of the expert evidence and ordered Mew to pay the GDC's costs [9].

Mew has disputed the ruling, saying the GDC offered as much scientific evidence for its approach as the Pope did in convicting Galileo, and that the regulator was more concerned with protecting the orthodontic industry [8].

Reported concerns about mewing as a self-directed practice are mainly jaw, neck or facial muscle strain, tooth movement or bite changes from sustained pressure, and speech effects [6][12]. Some looksmax.org users report temporomandibular joint symptoms from sustained posture [10]. Appliances used in clinical orthotropics carry the ordinary risks of oral appliances; the GDC findings concerned children fitted with expansion appliances and the ulceration and other harms recorded in the judgment [9].
Discover linked the wider looksmaxxing scene to higher-risk practices such as bonesmashing [4].

Orthotropics supplies much of the vocabulary used on looksmax.org for the face and jaws: 'craniofacial dystrophy', maxillary support, forward growth and tongue posture. A widely read guide describes craniofacial dystrophy as arising when the tongue is not resting on the palate, often through mouth breathing, so that the maxilla sinks down and back, producing 'tired eyes' and a recessed jaw [10].
Members trade reading lists and personal plans, and the discussion for adults often moves from posture to orthodontics, appliances and jaw surgery [14][13][10].

lore.intro: Orthotropics is the intellectual root of the mewing movement on looksmax.org, with users trading guides and treatment plans [14][10].
